entries.topic: Who the 2nd-3rd c. teachers of gnosis were: Simon, Basilides, Carpocratians, Valentinus and students, Sethians; the term; living Mandaeans; modern Gnostic churches

claims.text: Irenaeus (AH I.23) makes Simon Magus the source 'from whom all sorts of heresies derive their origin'; says Simon took Helena from a brothel in Tyre and called her the first conception of his mind, and that his followers had 'mystic priests', used magic and worshipped images of Simon as Jupiter and Helena as Minerva.

Irenaeus (AH I.24): Basilides taught Simon of Cyrene was crucified in Jesus' place while Jesus 'stood by and laughed'; 365 heavens whose chief is Abraxas; 'salvation belongs to the soul alone'; his followers ate idol meat 'without any hesitation'.
Irenaeus (AH I.25): the Carpocratians 'style themselves Gnostics'; Marcellina came to Rome under bishop Anicetus; they crowned images of Christ alongside Pythagoras, Plato and Aristotle.
Tertullian (Adv. Val. 4): Valentinus 'had expected to become a bishop' but another obtained it by a confessor's claim and he broke with the church; no city is named in the passage.
Tertullian (Prescr. 30): Marcion and Valentinus were believers in the Roman church under bishop Eleutherus and were expelled; Marcion's money brought into the church was returned to him.
Ptolemy's Letter to Flora survives complete in Epiphanius, Panarion 33.3-7; before Nag Hammadi it was one of the few authentic Gnostic works available.

'Gnosticism' was first coined in the 17th century by Henry More; scholars (Williams 1996, King 2003) dispute the category; Brakke and Pétrement treat it as intra-Christian in origin; Robinson: pre-Christian Gnosticism 'hardly attested'.

Sethianism is a modern scholarly category (Schenke among the first) for texts incl. Apocryphon of John, Zostrianos, Allogenes, Three Steles of Seth, Marsanes, Trimorphic Protennoia, Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit; its myth: unknown God, Barbelo, Sophia's act producing Yaldabaoth; 'Five Seals' rite read by Pearson as repeated immersion.

Mandaeans: 60,000-100,000 worldwide; Iraq c.5,000 by 2007 (c.3,000 per a 2019 estimate); c.90% of Iraqi Mandaeans killed or fled after 2003; John the Baptist their greatest teacher; repeated river baptism; Ginza Rabba; origins disputed.
Jules Doinel founded the Église Gnostique in Paris in autumn 1890 after visionary experiences (1888-89); resigned 1895, became Catholic and worked with Léo Taxil; readmitted 1900.

Marcion ascribed the Old Testament God and a second God of the Gospel to two principles; rejected elaborate creation myths and claimed no secret knowledge (Harnack rejects the Gnostic label; Mead accepts it; 1911 Britannica: a dualist but not a Gnostic); Marcionites founded churches across the Roman empire; canon of eleven books, a shorter Luke and ten Pauline epistles.

entries.topic: Core teachings: kingdom within, gnosis, demiurge, Sophia, spark, present resurrection, ascent, law, alchemy bridge

claims.text: Thomas 3: 'the kingdom is inside of you, and it is outside of you'; 113: the kingdom 'is spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it'; 70: what you have will save you if you bring it forth; 1: whoever finds the interpretation will not experience death.

Ramelli (2009) argues entos hymon in Luke 17:21 means 'inside you'; 'among' practically unattested; Vulgate intra vos; Peshitta 'inside'; Origen, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa read 'inside'; cites Thomas 3 and 113 as parallels.

Gospel of Mary (Berlin Codex): 'the Son of Man is within you'; 'I have given you no law, as the lawgiver did, lest you be bound by it'; 'Sin as such does not exist'; the soul passes powers incl. a fourth with seven forms of wrath; Peter: 'Did He prefer her to us?'

Apocryphon of John: Sophia brings forth without consent an imperfect being she names Yaltabaoth; he says 'I am a jealous God, and there is no other God beside me', which 'indicated... that there exists another God'; the saviour seals the awakened 'in the light of the water with five seals'; 'Cursed be everyone who will exchange these things for a gift or for food or for drink or for clothing'.

Gospel of Philip: 'Those who say they will die first and then rise are in error'; 'a baptism and a chrism and a eucharist and a redemption and a bridal chamber'; 'You saw Christ, you became Christ'; 'God is a dyer'.
Treatise on the Resurrection (to Rheginos): resurrection 'is no illusion, but it is truth'; 'already you have the resurrection'; 'why not consider yourself as risen'.

Irenaeus AH I.6: they divide people into material, animal (psychic) and spiritual; animal men need works and faith while the spiritual are saved 'because they are spiritual by nature'; they call church members 'animal'.

Irenaeus AH I.21: 'redemption' rites varied (spiritual marriage, baptism invoking the unknown Father, oil and water); the dying anointed to be 'incapable of being seized or seen by the principalities and powers' and taught words beginning 'I am a son from the Father'; some rejected rites: knowledge of the unspeakable Greatness 'is itself perfect redemption'.

Origen, Against Celsus VI.24-31: describes an Ophite diagram of ten circles, which he says he had seen ('the diagram which we possessed'), and formulas the soul addresses to archons Ialdabaoth, Iao, Sabaoth, Astaphaeus at their gates.

Zosimos of Panopolis (Akhmim), fl. c.300, wrote the oldest known alchemy books; framed transmutation as mirroring inner purification; used the Hermetic krater as baptismal symbol; fallen-angel metallurgy story shared with Enoch and Apocryphon of John.

Fraser (2007) argues Zosimos was a practising Hermetist drawing on Sethian works (Nikotheos, Zostrianos) to frame alchemical tincturing as baptism bringing gnosis; 'Zosimos discovers in the Hermetic writings an initiatory praxis'.

Ptolemy (Letter to Flora): God's law has three parts: the pure law (Decalogue) 'which the Savior came not to destroy but to complete'; law mixed with injustice, set aside; symbolic law (offerings, circumcision, sabbath, fasting, Passover) whose 'names remained the same but the content was changed'; true fasting is 'abstinence from everything evil'; 'the apostolic tradition which we too have received by succession'.

Ptolemy: the lawgiver is neither the perfect God nor the devil but 'the demiurge and maker of this universe', 'rightly given the name, intermediate', 'neither good nor evil or unjust, but can properly be called just'.
Jung wrote and privately published the Seven Sermons to the Dead in 1916, attributing them to Basilides of Alexandria.

entries.topic: Practice: rites, women, money, Sunday, rules; comparison with proto-orthodox practice

claims.text: Irenaeus AH I.13: Marcus has women consecrate mixed cups and tells a woman 'Open your mouth... and you shall prophesy'; alleges he targets women 'of great wealth' who give him their possessions, 'collected a very large fortune', and that some confessed being 'defiled by him' (hostile source).
Irenaeus AH III.15.2: Valentinians call church members 'ecclesiastic', imitate 'our phraseology', and complain that when 'they hold doctrines similar to ours' they are kept aloof and called heretics.

Tertullian Prescr. 41: among heretics 'it is doubtful who is a catechumen, and who a believer'; women 'bold enough to teach, to dispute, to enact exorcisms, to undertake cures—it may be even to baptize'; 'to-day one man is their bishop, to-morrow another'; 'on laymen do they impose the functions of priesthood'.

Thomas 6 and 14 reject or reinterpret fasting, prayer and almsgiving ('If you fast, you will give rise to sin for yourselves'); Thomas 27: if you do not keep the Sabbath as a Sabbath you will not see the Father; 53: true circumcision in spirit.
Justin, 1 Apol. 67 (c.155): Christians gather 'on the day called Sunday'; 'they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit'; the president 'succours the orphans and widows'.

Catholic Encyclopedia: clergy support at first 'supplied by the spontaneous offerings of the faithful'; earliest positive tithe legislation the bishops' letter at Tours 567 and canons of Mâcon 585; Charlemagne's capitularies the earliest civil enforcement.
Manichaeism: Elect took vows (no meat, wine); Hearers supplied them food; Diocletian's edict of 302 ordered Manichaean leaders burned with their writings; Augustine a Hearer c.9 years.
Irenaeus says Basilideans ate idol meat freely (I.24) and that Valentinian 'spirituals' attended pagan festivals and seduced women (I.6.3) — hostile allegations.

entries.topic: Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hippolytus, Epiphanius, Plotinus, Origen; Constantine's edict; Theodosian law; Pagels thesis and critics

claims.text: Irenaeus AH III.3: bishops instituted by the apostles traced 'to our own times'; Roman list Linus to Eleutherius 'in the twelfth place from the apostles'; 'every Church should agree with this Church, on account of its preeminent authority'.
Irenaeus's Against Heresies (c.180) states its aim of exposing teaching of 'knowledge falsely so called'.
Tertullian Prescr. 15, 19: he opposes 'admitting them to any discussion of the Scriptures'; 'Our appeal, therefore, must not be made to the Scriptures'; praescriptio is a Roman legal plea.

Refutation of All Heresies (early 3rd c.), attributed to Hippolytus or a 'Pseudo-Hippolytus'; books IV-X recovered 1842 from a Mount Athos manuscript; derives heresies from Greek philosophy; covers Naassenes, Peratae, Sethians, Valentinus, Basilides, Simon.

Epiphanius of Salamis began the Panarion in 374/375; 80 sects, compared to snakes; a 'medicine chest' against heresy's poisons; zeal sometimes kept him from examining doctrines closely; he admitted hearsay on Apollinarianism.

Plotinus, Ennead II.9 (Against the Gnostics): attacks contempt for the cosmos and its maker, multiplication of realities, salvation without moral effort, and their magic; Porphyry, Life 16 names Allogenes and Zostrianos.

Constantine's edict (Eusebius VC III.64-66) addressed 'Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulians, ye who are called Cataphrygians'; forbade them to assemble 'not in public merely, but in any private house or place whatsoever'; their houses of prayer to be 'made over without delay to the catholic Church'; 'search should be made for their books'.
Sozomen HE II.32 reports the same law: Novatians, Phrygians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulianists not to hold church in private houses or public places.

CTh 16.1.2 (380): heretics' gatherings 'shall not receive the name of churches'; CTh 16.5.1 (326) limits privileges to Catholics, heretics subject to fines; a CTh 16.5 law on Manichaeans fines leaders and confiscates meeting houses.

Pagels, The Gnostic Gospels (1979; National Book Award 1980): bodily resurrection doctrine 'serves an essential political function'; gnosis 'the theological justification for refusing to obey the bishops'; 'ideas alone do not make a religion powerful'. Critics: Chadwick (lacking 'full rigour'), McVey, Maccoby (idealises, skips elitism), Raymond Brown.
